daily_blocks.name: Warm-Up
details: 5 minutes of warm-up reduces injury risk by 70% — this isn't 'optional', it's mandatory. Cold muscles contract slowly, have less elasticity, and receive neural signals 30% slower.
Simple formula: joint rotations from top to bottom (neck → shoulders → hips → knees → ankles) 30 seconds each + 1 minute brisk walking or jumping jacks. Total 4–5 minutes is enough.
Even when rushed, maintain at least 3 minutes: rotate major joints + 10 jumping jacks + 5 arm circles per side. Never skip entirely.

daily_blocks.name: Main Workout
details: Mon/Wed/Fri = Strength (Squat, Hinge, Push, Pull, Core). Tue/Thu = Light Cardio (brisk walk, cycling, 100–130 bpm). Sat = Active Recovery. Sun = Complete rest.
Target RPE: 6–8/10. Not too easy (no adaptation stimulus) but not too hard (unable to recover). Record RPE immediately after each session.
Golden principle: form before volume, volume before intensity. Increase no more than 10% total volume per week to avoid overtraining.

points.label: RPE 6–8/10

daily_blocks.name: Cooldown Stretch
daily_blocks.desc: Static stretch · lower heart rate · relax muscles
details: After intense training, muscles are contracted. Static stretching 30s per muscle group helps restore muscle length and reduces DOMS (next-day soreness) by 20–30%.
Proper cool-down: slow walk 2 minutes → stretch → deep breathing. Don't sit or lie down immediately after heavy training — blood pooling in extremities can't return to the heart fast enough.
Foam rolling before static stretching (if available): 30 seconds per major muscle group. Priority: hamstrings, calves, hips, upper back. Better results than stretching alone.

Formula: 3 deep breaths (4s inhale – 4s hold – 6s exhale) → 2 minutes sitting quietly or silent walking → set 1 specific intention for the rest of the day.
If no time: 5 minutes silent walking (no phone, no music) is a complete substitute. Equivalent effect to seated meditation through Default Mode Network activation.

tips.title: Consistency Over Intensity
tips.desc: 3–5 sessions/week consistently beats one exhausting session. 20 minutes daily outperforms 2 hours monthly.
details: Consistency creates neural habit loops: the brain stops requiring willpower after 21–66 days of repetition — exercise becomes as automatic as brushing teeth. High intensity alone cannot create this.
Research from James Clear (Atomic Habits): people training 3 sessions × 20 min/week consistently for 1 year outperform those training 5 sessions × 60 min who quit after 3 months.
The 'never skip twice in a row' rule: skipping once = okay, twice in a row = habit starts breaking, three times = rebuild from scratch. Protecting the streak matters more than perfection.

points.label: Never skip twice
points.note: Simplest rule to maintain the habit

tips.title: Gradual Progressive Overload
tips.desc: Increase no more than 10% volume/week. This rule prevents injury and burnout long-term.
details: The '10% rule' is the golden principle of progressive overload: increase total volume (sets × reps × weight) by no more than 10% per week. Exceeding this doubles injury risk according to sports science research.
Practical example: if you train 100 'units' this week (10 sets × 10 reps) → max 110 next week. Don't increase weight + reps + sets simultaneously — change only one variable at a time.

Deload 1 week per month (reduce 40% volume): this isn't 'light training' — it's when the body supercompensates (recovers beyond baseline), emerging stronger. Skipping deloads costs 15–20% of long-term results.

points.label: Volume = sets×reps×weight
points.note: Track weekly total, not just per session

points.label: One variable at a time
points.note: Weight OR reps OR sets — not all three

tips.title: Sleep Is Recovery Medicine
tips.desc: 7–9h per night. Muscles grow during sleep, not during training. Sleep deprivation reduces performance by 20–30%.
details: Growth Hormone (GH) — the primary muscle-building and fat-burning hormone — is secreted 70% during deep sleep (slow-wave sleep). No deep sleep = no GH = gym training produces no results.
Sleeping only 6h (instead of 8h) for just one week: maximum strength drops 20%, testosterone falls 10–15%, cortisol rises 37%, motor skill learning capacity decreases 40%.

Sleep optimization isn't just about hours: quality matters more. Room temperature 18–20°C, complete darkness (blackout curtains), no phone 30 minutes before bed. Consistent bedtime = stable circadian rhythm.

tips.title: Enough Protein Daily
tips.desc: 1.6–2g protein/kg body weight. Prioritize whole foods: eggs, lean meat, tofu, Greek yogurt.
details: Protein is the only building material for muscle — without sufficient protein, no amount of training yields results. 1.6–2g/kg is the evidence-based range from a meta-analysis of 49 studies (Morton 2018).
Distribution matters more than total: 4–5 meals × 20–40g protein/meal stimulates protein synthesis more than 2 meals × 80g even with the same total. Breakfast ≥20g is particularly important.
Best protein sources: eggs (6g/egg), chicken breast (31g/100g), firm tofu (8–12g/100g), Greek yogurt (10g/100g), lentils (9g/100g cooked).

tips.title: Log Your Workouts
tips.desc: 5 min/session: record sets, reps, feeling. A training log reveals progress your eyes can't see.
details: A workout log is your 'progress map' — without it, you're driving without GPS. People who log their workouts reach fitness goals 42% faster than those who don't (AJPH 2012 study).
Minimum to record: exercise · weight · sets/reps · RPE (1–10) · general feeling. Log immediately after training while it's fresh — don't wait until the next day. App or notebook both work.
How to use your log: review every 4 weeks. RPE consistently 7–8 → increase load. RPE consistently 9–10 → reduce volume or deload. No progress → change rep range or exercise.

points.label: 5 min right after training
points.note: While you still remember — not next day

tips.title: Patience With Results
tips.desc: Real results come after 4–8 weeks of consistency. Early weeks are the brain learning — not laziness.
details: Weeks 1–3: the body is building new neural pathways — not creating new muscle but teaching the brain to control muscles more efficiently. Feeling 'still weak' is normal and a necessary step.
Weeks 4–6: neuromuscular adaptation completes — strength increases 20–40% without muscles getting bigger. This is why beginners feel dramatically stronger in the first 6 weeks.
Week 7+: hypertrophy (muscle size increase) begins to show. Body composition changes become visible. But 12 weeks of consistency are needed before others notice the change.

details: The 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) is the international medical standard for assessing cardiovascular endurance — used in clinical practice and sports research. Simple, requires no equipment, and accurate.
How to perform: find a straight flat path or sidewalk, walk as fast as possible for exactly 6 minutes (no running), measure total distance. Wear comfortable clothes and flat shoes.
Improvement targets: beginners typically improve 50–150m after 4 weeks of consistent training. Week 12: improving 150–300m is a good result. Healthy young adults: 500–700m/6 minutes.

points.label: Measure distance covered
points.note: Further in 6 minutes = better cardiovascular fitness

details: Maximum consecutive push-ups (without stopping) is the simplest and most reliable upper body strength test. Measures chest, shoulder, and tricep strength plus core stabilization simultaneously.

How to perform: standard push-up position (straight back, tight core), perform continuously without stopping until unable to complete one more full rep. Don't count reps with bent back or sagging hips.
Reference standards: men age 30 ≥25 reps = good, ≥35 = excellent. Women age 30 ≥15 reps = good, ≥25 = excellent. Beginners typically gain 5–15 reps after 8 weeks of proper training.

points.label: Full form required
points.note: Don't count reps with poor form

points.label: Chest · shoulder · tricep
points.note: 3 upper body muscle groups tested at once

details: The 1-minute Sit-to-Stand Test measures thigh and glute strength plus lower body neuromuscular coordination. This metric predicts fall risk and long-term quality of life.
How to perform: sit on an armless chair (43–46cm high), arms crossed on chest, stand up and sit down completely as many times as possible in exactly 1 minute.
Reference standards: men age 30 ≥23 reps = good. Women age 30 ≥21 reps = good. Beginners typically improve 5–10 reps/minute after 8 weeks. Below 14 reps/minute is a health warning threshold.
The Sit-and-Reach Test measures hamstring and lower back flexibility — the two tightest areas in sedentary people, directly related to back pain.

How to perform: sit on the floor with legs straight, slowly lean forward over 3 seconds to your maximum point without bending knees. Result: Yes = hands reach or pass toes. No = hands stop short of toes.
Going from 'No' → 'Yes' typically takes 4–8 weeks of consistent static stretching (30 seconds × 2 per session). This is one of the earliest visible improvements — great motivation for beginners.

points.label: Hamstrings + lower back
points.note: Two tightest areas for desk workers

points.label: Related to back pain
points.note: Tight hamstrings → anterior pelvic tilt → back pain

details: Morning weight before eating is the most consistent measurement: same conditions every time eliminates variables. Daily weight naturally fluctuates 1–2kg from water retention, food, hormones — look at weekly averages.
Track trends, not single numbers: weight trending downward over 4 weeks = success, even if individual days go up. Water weight changes can mask fat loss for 1–2 weeks.
Weigh at the same time, same conditions: after waking, after bathroom, before drinking or eating. Consistency of conditions matters far more than which scale you use.

details: Waist circumference is a stronger health predictor than BMI: it directly reflects visceral fat (fat around organs) — linked to cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome risk.
How to measure: stand relaxed, find your natural waist (between lower rib and hip bone), wrap tape horizontally. Measure after a natural exhale — not forced exhale, not holding breath.
Health targets: men <90cm (Asian standard) and women <80cm significantly reduce metabolic disease risk. Losing 5–10cm over 12 weeks of proper training and nutrition is a realistic goal.

A.title: Learn 6 Fundamental Movements

A.note: Perfect form before load. Don't worry about reps — that's your only goal today.

movesData.name: Squat — 3×12
details: Squat activates quads, glutes, and core simultaneously — the single best lower-body exercise. 3 sets × 12 reps with bodyweight or light load is the ideal starting point.
Key technique: knees track over toes, chest upright, sit hips back as if onto a chair. Never let knees cave inward.

movesData.name: Hinge (Deadlift) — 3×10
details: Hip hinge activates hamstrings, glutes, and lower back. Romanian Deadlift with light weight is the safest variant to start.
Technique: keep back straight, push hips back (not round the spine), feel hamstring stretch as you lower. Drive hips forward to stand.
This is the best exercise to prevent back pain — strong lower back = less pain from long sitting. 3×10 with good form beats heavy with poor form.

points.label: Prevents back pain

movesData.name: Push (Push-up) — 3×10
details: Push-ups activate chest, front deltoids, and triceps. No equipment needed — bodyweight is enough when form and tempo are controlled.
If floor push-ups are too hard: start with incline push-ups (hands on bench/wall), reduce angle as you get stronger. Never 'cheat' by arching your back.
3×10 with a 1-second pause at the bottom outperforms 3×20 fast reps. Paused push-up eliminates momentum — 100% muscle.

movesData.name: Pull (Row) — 3×10
details: Pull/Row activates mid-back, lats, and biceps. Balancing push with pull is the #1 rule to avoid shoulder injuries and upper back pain long-term.
Dumbbell row, resistance band row, or table row (no equipment) all work. Key: squeeze the mid-back on the pull — don't just use your arms.
Most beginners overtrain push and neglect pull — muscle imbalance leads to shoulder pain after 3–6 months. Keep a 1:1 push-to-pull ratio.

tipsData.name: Target Heart Rate 60–70% Max
details: Formula: max heart rate = 220 − age. Zone 2 cardio = 60–70% of max heart rate. Example age 30: max = 190 bpm → Zone 2 = 114–133 bpm.

Simplest way to gauge Zone 2 without devices: you must be able to say 1–2 complete sentences without gasping. Faster = Zone 3, slower = Zone 1.

faqs.q: Who is the Health & Lifestyle website for?
faqs.a: The website is for anyone who wants to improve their health — from complete beginners to those with a foundation looking to systematize their routine. No experience, no special equipment, no strict diet required. Just 20 minutes a day and consistency.

faqs.q: Is all content on the website completely free?
faqs.a: Yes — 100% free. All 6 pillars, 7-day / 12-week / 24-week programs, exercise videos, checklists, tracking tools and resources are completely free. Our goal is to make science-based health knowledge accessible to everyone without financial barriers.

faqs.q: Where should I start if I'm a complete beginner?
faqs.a: Start on the "Journey" page → choose "7-Day Kickstart". The first seven days are designed to gradually introduce all 4 core pillars (movement · nutrition · lifestyle · mind) without overwhelming you. Each day only requires 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: Is the content evidence-based?
faqs.a: Yes. All content is built on modern medical research and guidelines from reputable organizations (WHO, ACSM, AHA). However, this website is educational — it does not replace personal medical advice. If you have specific health concerns, consult a doctor.

faqs.q: What does the 360° Health system include?
faqs.a: 6 pillars form a comprehensive health system: (A) Movement & Exercise — strong body; (B) Nutrition & Meal Planning — right fuel; (C) Healthy Lifestyle — sleep, steps, recovery; (D) Calm Mind — emotional balance; (E) Health Knowledge — understand your body; (F) Tools & Resources — track and maintain.

faqs.q: How many times a week should I exercise?
faqs.a: For beginners, 3 sessions/week (every other day) is ideal. Recommended structure: 3 strength sessions · 2 light cardio · 2 active recovery days. More important than frequency is consistency — 3 regular sessions over 12 weeks beats 5 sessions/week for 2 weeks then quitting.

faqs.q: What are the 6 fundamental movements and why are they important?
faqs.a: 6 foundational movement patterns: Squat (knee bend), Hinge (hip fold), Push (press), Pull (row), Core (stability) and Breathe. These are the 6 movement groups the human body performs daily. Mastering these with proper form before adding load is rule #1 to prevent injury and build a sustainable foundation.

faqs.q: Can I follow the program without any equipment?
faqs.a: Absolutely. The entire Phase 1 program (7 days + first 4 weeks) uses 100% bodyweight — no equipment needed. From week 5 you can add dumbbells or resistance bands for extra challenge, but they are not required.

faqs.q: I have chronic back pain — can I still follow the program?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause and severity. The program includes "Active Recovery" and "Stretching" sections suitable for mild back pain. However, if back pain is caused by a spinal condition or is under medical treatment, consult a doctor or physiotherapist first. Golden rule: acute pain = rest; mild chronic pain = gentle controlled movement.

faqs.q: Do I have to count calories?
faqs.a: Not required, especially in the early stages. The "Plate Model" (½ vegetables · ¼ protein · ¼ carbs) and the "1 palm of protein per meal" rule help you eat right without counting. Calorie counting is only useful at an advanced stage when you want more precise optimization.

faqs.q: What is TDEE and do I need to calculate it?
faqs.a: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the total calories your body burns each day. Knowing your TDEE helps you eat the right amount for your goal: weight loss (TDEE − 400 kcal), maintenance (= TDEE), muscle gain (TDEE + 300 kcal). The TDEE calculator is in the B0 Toolkit on the Nutrition page.

faqs.q: I eat out a lot for work — can I still follow the nutrition guidelines?
faqs.a: Yes. The smart eating-out formula: "1 protein + 2 vegetables + moderate carbs". At restaurants: order extra vegetables or salad, choose grilled/steamed protein instead of fried, control carb portions. No need to refuse social meals — just apply a simple strategy.

faqs.q: Do I need to use supplements?
faqs.a: Not in the early stages. Whole foods are always the foundation — supplements only work when nutrition is already solid. If considering: Vitamin D3 (if rarely outdoors), Omega-3 (if low fish intake), Protein Whey (if struggling to get enough protein from food). Consult a doctor before taking any supplements.

faqs.q: How much water should I drink daily?
faqs.a: Simple formula: body weight (kg) × 35ml. Example: 60kg → 2.1 liters/day. Sign of adequate hydration: pale yellow urine. Add 500ml when exercising. Drink evenly throughout the day and start with a large glass of water immediately on waking.

faqs.q: How many hours of sleep do I need?
faqs.a: 7–9 hours is the recommendation for adults (WHO). More important than quantity is sleep quality and regularity — sleeping and waking at the same time every day (including weekends) matters more than sleeping extra on weekends to catch up.

faqs.q: What is NEAT and why is it more important than I think?
faqs.a: NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis) is the energy burned from all activities outside formal exercise — walking, standing, climbing stairs, doing chores. NEAT can account for 15–50% of total daily calories burned. Goal: 8,000–10,000 steps/day.

faqs.q: What does a minimal morning routine require?
faqs.a: A 10-minute morning routine is enough to make a difference: (1) Drink a large glass of water; (2) Get 5 minutes of natural sunlight; (3) Write 1 goal for the day. No need to wake up at 5 AM — just do it consistently.

faqs.q: How can I improve sleep quality fastest?
faqs.a: Three most effective interventions: (1) No screens 30 minutes before bed; (2) Keep bedroom at 18–22°C and completely dark; (3) No caffeine after 2 PM. Apply all three correctly for 7 days — you will notice a clear difference.

faqs.q: I've never meditated before — how do I start?
faqs.a: The simplest meditation: sit comfortably, close your eyes, focus on your breath for 5 minutes. When your mind wanders, gently bring attention back to your breath — without judgment. Start with 5 minutes each morning, gradually increasing to 10–15 minutes after 2 weeks.

faqs.q: What is Box Breathing and when should I use it?
faqs.a: Box Breathing: Inhale 4s → Hold 4s → Exhale 4s → Hold 4s → repeat. This technique activates the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing cortisol and heart rate within 2–3 minutes. Use when: stressed before a meeting, struggling to sleep, or before a workout.

faqs.q: I have no time to meditate — is there a way?
faqs.a: "Micro-meditation" works for busy lives: (1) 3 conscious deep breaths each morning (30 seconds); (2) Eat mindfully — no phone; (3) 5-minute mindful walk midday. These small moments add up to build a solid mental foundation.

faqs.q: What should I write in a health journal?
faqs.a: The 3-line evening journal formula (3–5 minutes): (1) "Today I did well..." — note 1 positive thing; (2) "I learned..." — 1 lesson or observation; (3) "Tomorrow I will..." — 1 specific action. After 4 weeks, looking back you will see your own patterns much more clearly.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 7-day, 12-week, and 24-week programs?
faqs.a: 7-Day Kickstart: Introduce all 4 pillars, form baseline habits. 12-Week Foundation: 3 phases building foundation → increasing load → personalizing. 24-Week Advanced: Expand to all 6 full pillars, including medical knowledge and carb cycling.

faqs.q: How much time do I need per day?
faqs.a: Daily Core structure 20–40 min: 5 min warm-up · 10–20 min main workout · 5–10 min cool-down · 5 min mind reset. Plus: 10-min morning routine + 5-min evening journal. Total: 35–55 min/day. No day requires more than 1 hour.

faqs.q: Can I skip the 7 days and go straight to the 12-week program?
faqs.a: You can, but it is not recommended. The first 7 days help you understand how your body responds to change, identify weaknesses, and build psychological momentum. People who skip the 7 days tend to quit earlier. If you already have a solid base (consistent training for 6+ months), you can start from Phase 2 of the 12-week program.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss 1–2 days in the program?
faqs.a: No worries. The rule: "Never miss twice in a row". Miss 1 day → continue from the next day, no need to make up. Miss 1 week → restart from the beginning of that week. 80% consistency over 12 weeks beats 100% for 3 weeks then quitting.

faqs.q: What is the BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) formula?
faqs.a: BMR uses the Mifflin-St Jeor formula: Male = (10 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (5 × age) + 5. Female = (10 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (5 × age) − 161. Example: Male 30 years, 70kg, 170cm → BMR = 700 + 1062.5 − 150 + 5 = 1617.5 kcal/day. This is the minimum energy your body needs at complete rest.

faqs.q: How is TDEE calculated? What are the activity multipliers?
faqs.a: TDEE = BMR × Activity Multiplier. Levels: Sedentary (desk job, no exercise) × 1.2; Light (1–3 sessions/week) × 1.375; Moderate (3–5 sessions/week) × 1.55; Active (6–7 sessions/week) × 1.725; Very Active (2× daily training) × 1.9. Example: BMR 1617 kcal × 1.55 (moderate) = 2506 kcal TDEE.

faqs.q: How many calories should I eat based on my goal?
faqs.a: Adjust from your TDEE: Weight loss = TDEE − 400 kcal (moderate deficit, not extreme); Maintenance = TDEE; Muscle gain = TDEE + 300 kcal (small surplus). Never eat below your BMR. Example with TDEE 2500: weight loss = 2100 kcal, muscle gain = 2800 kcal.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my macro ratios (protein, fat, carbs)?
faqs.a: Step 1 — Protein: body weight × 1.6–2.0g (use 2.0g for weight loss or muscle gain; 1.6g for maintenance). Step 2 — Fat: 25% of total calories ÷ 9 (since 1g fat = 9 kcal). Step 3 — Carbs fill the rest: (Total kcal − Protein×4 − Fat×9) ÷ 4. Example: 70kg, 2100 kcal weight loss — Protein 140g (560 kcal) · Fat 58g (525 kcal) · Carbs 254g (1016 kcal).

faqs.q: What is the caloric density of each macronutrient?
faqs.a: Key constants: Protein = 4 kcal/g; Carbohydrates = 4 kcal/g; Fat = 9 kcal/g; Alcohol = 7 kcal/g (nearly as dense as fat, often overlooked). Practical examples: 100g chicken breast (30g protein) ≈ 120 kcal; 100g cooked rice (28g carbs) ≈ 130 kcal; 1 tablespoon cooking oil (14g fat) ≈ 126 kcal.

faqs.q: How much water do I need? What is the water intake formula?
faqs.a: Basic formula: body weight (kg) × 35ml = minimum daily water intake. Examples: 60kg × 35 = 2,100ml (2.1 liters); 75kg × 35 = 2,625ml (2.6 liters). Add: +500ml per workout session; +300ml in hot weather. Signs of adequate hydration: pale yellow urine. Signs of dehydration: dark yellow urine, dry mouth, fatigue.

faqs.q: How is BMI calculated and what do the ranges mean?
faqs.a: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ [height (m)]². Example: 68kg, 1.70m → BMI = 68 ÷ (1.70)² = 23.5. WHO classifications: Under 18.5 = Underweight; 18.5–24.9 = Normal; 25.0–29.9 = Overweight; 30.0+ = Obese. Note: BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat — muscular people may be classified as "overweight" despite excellent health. Combine with waist circumference (<90cm men, <80cm women) for more accurate assessment.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my training heart rate zones?
faqs.a: Maximum Heart Rate (HRmax) = 220 − age. Example: age 30 → HRmax = 190 bpm. Heart rate zones: 50–60% HRmax = Light warm-up (minimal aerobic benefit); 60–70% HRmax = Optimal fat-burning zone; 70–85% HRmax = Cardio zone — improves cardiovascular fitness; 85–95% HRmax = Advanced zone — for experienced athletes only. For beginners: aim for 60–75% HRmax for 20–30 minutes.

b5.body_comp_warn_title: Why do you lose muscle when cutting too aggressively?
b5.body_comp_warn_body: When the deficit exceeds 600 kcal/day, the body breaks down muscle protein (gluconeogenesis) to produce glucose. This is why protein ≥1.8g/kg and strength-maintenance training are MANDATORY when losing fat.
